title: Alpha School is developing a book-rich, knowledge-rich curriculum. Ask me how I know.
author: Karen Vaites
summary: Karen Vaites, a longtime advocate for knowledge-rich curriculum, announces that she has been working part time as an early-reading specialist on Alpha School's Learning Science team. She explains how a call from Carl Hendrick overcame her scepticism about first-generation ed-tech and says the Alpha Phonics app changed her view of what AI-era tools can do. She describes Alpha as a startup with a closed-loop system in which it builds apps, its own students use them, and results are measured daily. She argues that the useful question is whether learning scientists can build a coherent curriculum, instruction, and assessment system for any population, not only whether past results were real. She corrects common misconceptions, for example that pupils learn from chatbots, and sets ground rules for how she will engage with critics. The post is part personal declaration and part defence of a new norm for discussing Alpha.
points: Vaites says her decision followed years of frustration that advocacy, even a well-received playbook for reading reform, produced little action compared with the attention given to Alpha.
She frames Alpha as a startup whose closed-loop model lets it build, test, and measure apps daily, making it a powerful research and development platform.
She argues that quality ed-tech was never about the screen but about content, learning experience, and instructional design.
She clarifies that Alpha's platform blocks open internet and chatbots for students, and says Alpha students spend less time on devices than many public school students.
She asks critics to stop harassing educators who join disruptive startups and says her team will explain learning science rather than answer for every part of Alpha.
quotes: Alpha designs the school experience around a compressed “two hour learning” academic block, using AI-enabled, personalized apps to streamline the learning experience.
So most Alpha discourse consists of people reacting to the idea of Alpha, based on their priors.

This brings me to Alpha’s biggest advantage: we have a closed-loop ecosystem. Meaning: we build the apps, our own students use them, and we carefully measure their progress, so we have daily insight into what’s working and what isn’t.
Let me be clear. I want a knowledge-building, book-rich curriculum for every child in America, starting in kindergarten.
Two things can be true: the overwhelming majority of first-generation EdTech was terrible. Also, AI creates new breakthrough opportunities to personalize learning, and they are worth embracing.
It was never about the screens… it was about the content, the learning experience, the instructional design.

the better question is: can the world’s best learning scientists create a comprehensive, cohesive curriculum, instruction, and assessment system that can deliver breakthrough outcomes regardless of the student population?
